description: How social loafing, deindividuation and morality shape prosocial and antisocial crowd behaviour.
content_html:
Behaviour in Crowds

Being part of a crowd changes how people behave. Sometimes crowds act heroically — rushing to help in a disaster, organising community aid. Other times they act destructively — rioting, looting, or enabling harm to continue. Psychologists study what causes this shift between prosocial and antisocial crowd behaviour.

Prosocial behaviour in crowds includes collective acts that benefit others — for example, people spontaneously forming bucket chains to fight a fire, or audiences donating at a charity event. Antisocial behaviour in crowds includes aggression, vandalism, looting and violence directed at others.

Social Factors Affecting Collective Behaviour

Three key social factors shape how people behave in crowds: social loafing, deindividuation and culture.

Social loafing occurs when individuals exert less effort in a collective task because they assume others will make up the shortfall. The larger the group, the less any single person feels their contribution matters. In crowd contexts, social loafing can explain why individual moral responsibility is diluted — no one feels personally accountable for the group’s actions, whether those are helpful or harmful.

Deindividuation happens when being part of a crowd causes a person to lose their sense of individual identity. When people feel anonymous within a large group — especially when wearing uniforms, masks or being in darkness — the usual self-monitoring and moral constraints weaken. This can release both prosocial behaviour (people feel free to give generously at a concert) and antisocial behaviour (people feel free to behave violently at a riot).

The key mechanism of deindividuation is reduced personal accountability. Because no one knows who you are, you feel less responsible for what you do as part of the crowd. The crowd’s mood and norms fill the space left by the individual’s normal conscience.

Culture shapes the norms and expectations that govern crowd behaviour. Different societies have different traditions for collective gatherings. In some cultures, large crowds are expected to be orderly and quiet; in others, lively collective expression is the norm. Cultural background also affects how much an individual values group solidarity over personal action, which in turn affects how much they conform to the crowd’s prevailing behaviour.

Key Fact

The three social factors affecting collective behaviour are social loafing (reduced individual effort), deindividuation (loss of personal identity and accountability) and culture (learned norms for group behaviour). Deindividuation can lead to both prosocial and antisocial outcomes depending on the crowd’s prevailing mood.

Dispositional Factors Affecting Collective Behaviour

Even within the same crowd, individuals differ in how they behave. Two dispositional factors help explain these differences: personality and morality.

Personality affects behaviour in crowds. People who are high in traits such as agreeableness or empathy are more likely to behave prosocially even in a crowd where antisocial norms are emerging. Those who are highly susceptible to group influence, or who have low self-control, are more likely to be swept along by antisocial crowd behaviour.

Morality is the other key dispositional factor. Individuals with well-developed personal moral standards are more likely to resist antisocial crowd behaviour, even when deindividuation or social loafing reduce accountability. A person who strongly values fairness or compassion may step forward to protect a victim even in a hostile crowd, precisely because their internal moral framework overrides the crowd’s influence.

Key Fact

Dispositional factors — personality and morality — explain why individuals in the same crowd behave differently. Strong personal morality can override deindividuation, enabling individuals to act against the crowd’s antisocial norms.

Evaluating Explanations of Collective Behaviour

A strength of using deindividuation to explain crowd behaviour is that it can account for both prosocial and antisocial outcomes depending on the crowd’s dominant norms, making it a flexible explanation. Research from carnival settings shows deindividuation can increase generosity, not only aggression.

A weakness of focusing on social factors is that it may overstate the uniformity of crowd behaviour. In practice, crowds are rarely homogeneous — different individuals within the same crowd make different choices, which suggests dispositional factors such as morality and personality are also important. A complete explanation of collective behaviour needs both situational and dispositional perspectives.

Social loafing is well-supported by laboratory research, but may be less pronounced when individuals feel their contributions are uniquely important or when tasks are personally meaningful. The effect is not inevitable, and understanding its limits is important for applying it to real-world crowd settings.

An integrated understanding of collective behaviour recognises that social and dispositional factors do not operate independently — they interact. A person with strong moral values placed in an extreme situation of deindividuation may still be swept along if the social loafing effect is strong enough. Conversely, even low-morality individuals may behave prosocially in a crowd with strong prosocial norms. The best predictions about collective behaviour come from considering both what kind of person is present and what kind of crowd situation they are in.
exam_tip_html: The examiner report warns that students sometimes design a study on bystander behaviour when the question asks about antisocial crowd behaviour, or fail to include the dispositional element (personality or morality) when it is specified. Read the question carefully — if it says “dispositional factors”, your answer must name personality or morality and explain them. Don’t just write about social loafing and deindividuation.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Collective behaviour in crowds is shaped by social factors: social loafing (reduced individual effort), deindividuation (loss of identity and accountability) and culture (learned group norms).
  • Dispositional factors — personality and morality — explain why individuals in the same crowd respond differently, with strong morality able to override antisocial crowd norms.
  • Deindividuation can produce both prosocial and antisocial outcomes; a full explanation of crowd behaviour requires both social and dispositional perspectives.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes deindividuation?
A) Working harder when observed by others in a crowd
B) Feeling greater personal responsibility in a large group
C) Losing individual identity and sense of personal accountability in a crowd
D) Deliberately choosing to help others in an anonymous setting
practice_questions.marks: C) Losing individual identity and sense of personal accountability in a crowd [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define 'social loafing' as it applies to collective behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to put in less effort when part of a group [1 mark] because they assume that others will make up for their reduced contribution [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how deindividuation can lead to antisocial behaviour in crowds.
practice_questions.marks: Deindividuation occurs when people lose their individual identity within a crowd [1 mark]. This reduces personal accountability — because individuals feel anonymous, the self-monitoring and moral constraints that usually govern behaviour weaken [1 mark]. As a result, people are more likely to follow the crowd’s prevailing antisocial norms, such as joining in aggression or vandalism [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: At a music festival, some concert-goers behave antisocially, vandalising stalls. Others in the same crowd are helpful and look after strangers. Using your knowledge of collective behaviour, explain why people in the same crowd might behave so differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two factors precisely identified and linked to the scenario (e.g. deindividuation — the large crowd and anonymity of the festival reduce personal accountability, allowing antisocial behaviour; morality — individuals with strong personal values of fairness resist the crowd’s antisocial norms and act helpfully instead).
Secure: One factor clearly explained and linked to the scenario.
Developing: Names a relevant concept but does not connect it clearly to the scenario.
Emerging: Vague reference to crowd influence without psychological framing.

practice_questions.text: Describe the social factors that affect collective behaviour in crowds.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate, detailed description of all three social factors (social loafing, deindividuation, culture) with psychological terminology; clear explanation of how each factor operates in a crowd context; coherent organisation.
Secure: Describes two or three social factors with reasonable accuracy and some development.
Developing: Describes one or two factors with limited development.
Emerging: Brief, vague or inaccurate description of one factor.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the social and dispositional factors that affect crowd and collective behaviour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of social factors (social loafing, deindividuation, culture) and dispositional factors (personality, morality); evaluation covers at least two developed points (e.g. deindividuation explains both prosocial and antisocial outcomes; but social factors alone cannot account for individual variation within a crowd — dispositional factors are also needed; social loafing effect is not universal).
Secure: Description of most factors; evaluation covers two points with some development.
Developing: Describes a few factors; evaluation present but underdeveloped.
Emerging: Brief description; minimal evaluation.

options: Working harder because others are watching
The loss of individual identity and personal accountability in a crowd
Choosing to obey an authority figure in a group setting
The increase in personal effort when group tasks are difficult

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a dispositional factor affecting collective behaviour?
_____ loafing occurs when individuals put in less effort within a group because they expect others to compensate.
Individuals with strong personal _____ are more likely to resist antisocial crowd behaviour even when deindividuation reduces accountability.
Match each concept to its description:
right: Reduced individual effort when part of a collective task
Loss of personal identity and accountability within a crowd
Personal standards of right and wrong that can override crowd influence

flashcard_questions.q: What is prosocial behaviour in the context of crowd psychology?
flashcard_questions.a: Collective actions that benefit others, such as helping or cooperating in a crowd.

flashcard_questions.q: What is antisocial behaviour in the context of crowd psychology?
flashcard_questions.a: Behaviour in a crowd that harms others, such as aggression, vandalism or violence.
Individuals exert less effort in a group, assuming others will compensate.
Loss of individual identity and personal accountability when part of a crowd.

flashcard_questions.q: How does deindividuation lead to antisocial crowd behaviour?
flashcard_questions.a: Anonymity weakens self-monitoring and moral constraints, allowing crowd norms to dominate.

flashcard_questions.q: Can deindividuation lead to prosocial as well as antisocial behaviour?
flashcard_questions.a: Yes — if the crowd's dominant norm is generous or helpful, deindividuation can amplify that too.

flashcard_questions.q: How does morality affect collective behaviour?
flashcard_questions.a: Strong personal morality can override crowd pressure and lead individuals to resist antisocial norms.

flashcard_questions.q: How does personality affect collective behaviour?
flashcard_questions.a: Empathetic or agreeable personalities are more likely to behave prosocially even in an antisocial crowd.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one weakness of social loafing as an explanation of crowd behaviour.
flashcard_questions.a: Loafing is reduced when individuals feel their contribution is uniquely important or personally meaningful.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do people in the same crowd sometimes behave very differently?
flashcard_questions.a: Dispositional factors — personality and morality — mean individuals respond differently to the same crowd norms.

glossary_terms.definition: Behaviour that benefits others or society, such as helping, cooperating or sharing.
Behaviour that harms others or society, such as aggression, vandalism or violence.
The tendency for individuals to put in less effort when working as part of a group than they would when working alone.
The loss of individual identity and personal responsibility that can occur in a crowd, leading to a reduced sense of accountability for one's actions.
Stable individual characteristics that influence how a person responds to social situations, including crowd membership.
An individual's personal standards of right and wrong, which can either reinforce or counteract the influence of the crowd on behaviour.
